lead.t: Strabismus, nystagmus, and optic atrophy are common in children with CP; an ophthalmologist should be included in the initial assessment and ongoing treatment.

b: Nystagmus is involuntary rhythmic eye movement. It can be horizontal, vertical or torsional.
Assess its direction, whether it changes with gaze and whether it occurs spontaneously or with positional testing.
Possible causes include vestibular disease, cerebellar disease, drug toxicity and brainstem disorders.
Vertical or direction-changing gaze-evoked nystagmus can raise concern for a central cause, particularly when accompanied by other neurological signs.

qs.q: A 40-year-old man presents with vertigo brought on by changing head positions, lasting less than a minute. Dix-Hallpike maneuver elicits rotary nystagmus and delayed onset vertigo. What is the pathological mechanism?
o: Increased endolymph volume causing dilation of the membranous semicircular duct.
Free-floating otoconia displaced into the posterior semicircular canal (canalithiasis).
Viral reactivation leading to inflammation of the vestibular nerve.
Perilymph leakage through a fistula at the oval window.
Ischemic reduction of blood flow to the brainstem vestibular nuclei.
qs.e: BPPV is caused by canalithiasis where otoconia migrate into the semicircular canal.

qs.q: A chronic alcoholic presents with truncal ataxia, unsteady gait, and nystagmus. Histology reveals granule cell loss and Bergmann gliosis. Where is the principal site of cerebellar degeneration?
qs.e: Chronic alcoholic cerebellar degeneration predominantly affects the granule cells in the superior anterior vermis, leading to Bergmann gliosis. The base of the pons is the site affected in osmotic demyelination syndrome.
